item.title: Portal 2 (2011) - ★★★★½
item.description:
A timeless, modern masterpiece
After finally experiencing Portal and loving it, I finally played Portal 2 and found it equally impressive, bigger and better in every way: the graphics, the narrative evolution, the mechanics, and more complex puzzles, even though a part of me still really missed the simplicity of the first one. GLaDOS's development is brilliant, as are the plot twists and the introduction of Wheatley, a new character who embodies the impact of absolute power on weak minds (a very timely parallel to political movements that are still happening today). There is also the deeper look into Cave Johnson, representing corporate greed, blind optimism, and a total lack of ethics (equally timely). The resolution of the story is fantastic. It’s a super contemporary and modern game. Beyond the story, the gameplay is a masterclass in how to introduce increasingly complex mechanics without a single tutorial; it’s all about experimentation, trial and error, combining "powers" that make the puzzles more and more complex to solve, yet entirely doable at the same time. I find it impressive how well balanced the challenge level in this game is. In puzzle games, it's very hard to strike that balance: some are frustratingly difficult (plus, developers nowadays pretty much expect you to look up tips and tutorials online); other games are too simple, lacking any challenge and becoming equally frustrating. I’m far from a genius at these types of games, but in both 1 and 2, I managed to solve everything with absolutely no help, which is very rare, while still feeling challenged and engaged. Some took a bit longer, so I’d leave them aside and the answer would hit me the next day, but on average, it was perfect. One more classic checked off my eternal backlog, and I'm glad to finally understand the reason behind its historical importance.

item.title: Final Fantasy XVI (2023) - ★★★½
item.description:
The higher the peak, the deeper the valley.
Final Fantasy is one of those franchises where I still want to play all the mainline games. I love the whole mystique behind it, being one of the most classic series in gaming history, dating back to the 80s. Back then, I played some of the early titles, but with a childhood mindset: it was just another game we casually enjoyed, playing it repeatedly without ever finishing. We didn't really understand what was going on, partly due to age, but mostly because of the language barrier. There were no translations back then, and my 10, 11, or 12 year old self didn't speak English, let alone Japanese. But regardless of that, just like Mario and Zelda, it’s a series that has been present throughout my life. Even if you haven't played them all, you end up nurturing a deep affection for these characters over the years. That being said, I’ve only played a few Final Fantasy games like 6, 7 Remake, and 15, so not enough to join the heated debate about what is or isn't a "real Final Fantasy" (especially now that the gameplay has shifted to a hack-and-slash). For me, this specific title has some of the highest and grandest highs I’ve ever seen in a videogame, but the lows are also incredibly deep. It’s a game with a very obvious pacing problem. It goes from a frantic agility with music video style editing and Devil May Cry esque fights during main bosses to a completely slow and dragged down rhythm in the moment to moment gameplay, especially during sidequests. One hour you are fighting in space against colossal Eikons and bosses that literally split the seas; the next, you are serving food at tables, picking flowers, and gathering dirt. I’m not against mundane sidequests. I think it’s valid to use them to feel the day to day life of that world, learn the NPCs' routines, and grow to care about them. However, even in the secondary missions with interesting stories (like the one with the wolf and the nobleman's son), the mechanics are just too mundane. In the end, you are always doing the exact same thing. There were many moments where I caught myself thinking about giving up, completely bored. Even though the combat is engaging, the regular encounters don't demand much from you. On the flip side, at other moments I would think, "Wow, I’m being unfair to this game, what I’m seeing on screen is incredible!". The soundtrack and the major battles are increasingly impactful and memorable. The issue is that since the game is so long, these peaks are spaced too far apart. To be fair, closer to the end, the experience gets much more interesting. The conclusion of the main characters' sidequests is very well done and emotional the game is extremely well written. I also really enjoyed the battle trial system and even the "Monster Hunter" style hunts. All in all, I feel like this could easily be a 5/5 game if it had been edited down to highlight only its best parts. Unfortunately, that brilliance ends up diluted across hours and hours of uninteresting content.

item.title: Back to the Future: The Game (2010) - ★★★
item.description:
The fourth BTTF movie that never existed
This game is a combination of two nostalgic worlds for me. Back to the Future was one of the movies of my childhood. Its trilogy is timeless and still holds up today. And on the other side, there are Point and Click games, which were a big part of my early teenage years, with games like Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle, Full Throttle… In other words, I am definitely the target audience for this game, just like many other people who grew up in the 80s and 90s. I believe this factor is very important to my impression of the game, because if you don't fit into this profile, you probably won't enjoy it nearly as much.
In terms of story, this is an extremely valuable experience for anyone who is nostalgic for the movies and would like to see a new story set in this rich universe with these beloved characters. The story is genuinely good and has the right tone, and having Christopher Lloyd, Michael J. Fox, and Thomas F. Wilson involved makes everything even more special. The moments when the original movie soundtrack kicks in give me chills.
It's very rare nowadays to see a game bring a franchise from another medium into the gaming world with this much attention to detail. With all the difficulties involved in licensing, this has become almost impossible, so much so that the game itself was eventually delisted after losing its license.
As a Point and Click game, it's okay, with some decent puzzles that often rely on somewhat forced logic, but that's also something relatively common in this genre. There are still some genuinely good moments.
For me, the biggest problem with this game is the gameplay. And not just because it's a 15 year old game. I believe the gameplay was already bad even for its time. This becomes even more noticeable because it's a Point and Click game played on a console, something that has always been a challenge and is still difficult to get right even today. Return to Monkey Island, from 2022, might be the peak of this kind of adaptation.
Everything feels very clunky, with more buttons than there should be, the movement is stiff, and this combination makes exploration, which is such an important part of this type of game, feel much more outdated and tedious than it should. If it weren't for the licensing issues, this would be a great candidate for a remake. Improving the gameplay and adding some quality of life features could turn it into a much better game.
As it stands today, I would only recommend it to people who already have some experience with Point and Click games and, most importantly, to anyone who loves Back to the Future.

item.title: Nine Sols (2024) - ★★★★½
item.description:
The pinnacle of (2D) combat mechanics
Finally, I played the famous “2D Sekiro,” expecting exactly that: difficulty and parrying. But I ended up discovering a game that is so much more than that.
Yes, it has both of those elements and a lot of them. In my opinion, it can be even more demanding than Sekiro at times. But it also has a unique and incredible story, secondary characters you genuinely care about, beautiful art, and very satisfying exploration.
The game is a metroidvania focused on combat, especially boss fights, and it does this brilliantly. It knows exactly where to demand your energy.
The exploration itself isn’t particularly complex, but it’s really enjoyable, especially after defeating a boss. It’s that moment when you just want to take a breath, open the map, explore a little, and grab some upgrades. Even the regular enemies, for the most part, aren’t particularly difficult.
The minibosses, on the other hand, are a huge difficulty spike. Many of them are just as difficult as the actual bosses. And, in my opinion, the game does this intentionally. That’s where it wants you to stop, learn, spend your energy, and master the combat.
I think this is exactly where many smaller games that try to be Soulslikes get it wrong: they want to be difficult all the time, in absolutely everything. And that ends up making the game feel slow and tedious, but not in a good way. I felt this while playing Souldiers, for example. At some point, I just couldn’t take it anymore. It felt like nothing was progressing.
Nine Sols doesn’t make that mistake. It knows when to push you and when to let you breathe. And that kept me engaged for pretty much the entire game.
Because of that, it has become one of my favorite indie games of all time and maybe one of the hardest games I’ve ever played.
The boss fights, for the most part, are extremely demanding. They force you to master every mechanic in the game to its absolute limit. With many of them, you’ll spend hours trying, learning their patterns, understanding their openings, and, most importantly, improving your execution.
But the most important thing is that every single one of these fights is genuinely interesting. Learning each one is incredibly satisfying. And when you finally win, there’s no feeling that you got lucky or that the game simply gave it to you. You know you won because you actually learned how to beat it.
And when that happens, it’s pure bliss.

item.title: Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy (2021) - ★★★½
item.description:
Like a popcorn movie
A fun and enjoyable game. Definitely worth playing when you’re looking for something lighter and more laid back, without too much commitment. It’s funny and got a few genuine laughs out of me, with a very "Marvel Movie like" sense of humor. However, towards the end, I was getting a little tired of the jokes based on each character’s stereotypes. The characters themselves, though, are very charismatic, with an interpersonal dynamic that works really well.
The gameplay is quite solid. You play as Peter Quill and give commands to the rest of the team: Gamora, Drax, Groot, and Rocket. What I enjoyed the most was the visual presentation. It’s a beautiful and colorful game, with extremely creative worlds and creatures, and graphics that are above average. Another standout is the ’80s soundtrack. Even though I find the choice a little cliché, it’s genuinely very good, with songs I didn’t expect to hear in an action game.
In the end, for me, it’s a feel-good game, something that I had a lot of fun playing, but probably not a game that will stay with me.

item.title: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice - Game of the Year Edition (2020) - ★★★★★
item.description:
The pinnacle of combat mechanics
I started my FromSoftware Souls journey in 2022 with Bloodborne, then moved on to Demon’s Souls, Dark Souls 1, 2, and 3, Elden Ring, and finally Sekiro.
This has definitely become my favorite subgenre of the last decade, maybe even of my life. I love the exploration, the challenges, and, most importantly, the way these games reward you proportionally to how much you dedicate yourself to them. There’s a sense of accomplishment that very few other genres can provide. A lot of people criticize these games for their difficulty, as if it were something toxic or purely for showing off (maybe the community is a little bit like that). I see it differently. Difficulty is necessary for these games to work. They demand your attention, and death isn’t just a punishment, it’s a gameplay mechanic. Once you understand that, your relationship with frustration changes completely. I’m far from being an exceptional player, but I really enjoy the learning process that each FromSoftware game demands, each in its own way.
That said, the reason I left Sekiro for last was precisely because I was afraid it would be too difficult. On practically every list I came across, it was considered the hardest FromSoftware game. Today, I find that pretty debatable. In my experience, the hardest game is usually the first one you play, because this subgenre has its own logic that can be confusing at first. After playing all of them, I find their difficulty levels to be surprisingly close.
So why does Sekiro have this reputation? Mainly because it forces you to learn its combat system. The posture system, parrying, and Mikiri Counter are essential. In the other Souls games, there are several ways to work around a challenge, you can change your build, use a different weapon, level up, or find another strategy. In Sekiro, there’s not quite as much room for that. To finish the game, you have to get good at it.
This creates a huge initial barrier, even for someone who has already played several FromSoftware games. But once you get past it, I’m not sure it’s actually the hardest. There are some very difficult bosses, but this wasn’t the game where I spent the most time stuck on a boss, thinking I would never be able to beat it. On average, the bosses are difficult, but, for me, their highest difficulty spikes don’t come close to something like Malenia.
I also find the replay factor interesting. I ended up playing all the other games three or four times because of the platinum trophies. Sekiro might actually be the easiest to replay precisely because, when you come back to it, you already understand its mechanics and know the bosses’ moves. I’d say it is, by far, the hardest to learn, but once you master it, it becomes one of the easiest to replay.
Putting the difficulty aside, Sekiro’s combat mechanics might be one of the most incredible things I’ve ever experienced in a game. The moment to moment gameplay in every fight is a delight. Landing a perfect parry feels incredible. The Mikiri Counter is even better; even basic enemies can turn into genuinely epic encounters.
The exploration also works really well. The grappling hook makes the world more vertical and the movement extremely dynamic. Everything feels incredibly fluid without ever allowing you to go into autopilot mode. Another interesting change is the narrative, which is much more direct, contained, and clear than in the other FromSoftware games. And I really liked that.
I loved Sekiro. A masterpiece. I already miss it. After making my way through FromSoftware’s entire Souls lineup, I think it’s finally time to explore other franchises in the same vein.

item.title: Portal (2007) - ★★★★
item.description:
The AI dilemma
Portal is one of those classics you always hear about, especially because of its historical importance to puzzle games and its reputation as a reference point for narrative design. Since it was released in 2007, almost 20 years ago, I went into it with something of a historian’s mindset: trying to understand the context, the limitations of the time, the different pacing, and the mechanics that might feel dated today. And… to my surprise, I found almost none of that.
The gameplay and the “rules of the game” are extremely simple, but incredibly inventive. During the first few chambers, I thought it was okay, fun, interesting, but I assumed there wouldn’t be much more that could be done with such a simple mechanic. Once again, I was wrong. Without gaining new powers, weapons, or upgrades, the game becomes increasingly complex and creative, constantly asking you to solve puzzles using essentially the same abilities you had from the very beginning.
Another major highlight is the narrative, especially the oppressive atmosphere and the character of GLaDOS. A character created almost 20 years ago who speaks to a subject that feels incredibly relevant today, Artificial Intelligence.
GLaDOS is the HERAT of the game. While you are using your BRAIN to solve the puzzles, she is the one pushing you forward, challenging you, and shaping the entire experience. And the most impressive part is that, until the very end, she is essentially just a voice. She doesn't need a face, perfect graphics, or spectacular visual effects to become such a memorable presence. She is simply a voice and an extremely well written script.
As the game progresses, you begin to understand what is really happening and how this character gradually becomes the villain of the story. She lies to you, manipulates you, makes passive-aggressive comments, and eventually tries to kill you, just as she did with everyone who took the test before you.
And this is where I find the parallel between GLaDOS and today's generative AI particularly interesting: trust, objectives, manipulation, and dependency.
In the game, we discover that the humans working at Aperture were killed. In our world, the concerns are different, but the questions surrounding AI are also about its impact on human beings: the replacement of workers, jobs, social and environmental consequences, and so many other issues.
The promise of the cake works almost like a perfect metaphor, “Do this and you will receive that.” There is a reward promised at the end, and that expectation is what keeps you following GLaDOS's instructions. The problem is that, as you progress, you realize that you cannot completely trust the person making the promise. And perhaps that's why GLaDOS feels so strangely relevant today. She isn't just an AI that wants to kill you. She is an AI that asks you to trust her while controlling the environment, defining the rules, and deciding what information you receive.
The cake was never really the lie. The lie was believing the system had your best interests in mind.

item.title: The Wolf Among Us (2013) - ★★★★
item.description:
Now I get the hype
I knew next to nothing about The Wolf Among Us before playing, so the whole premise of taking characters from our childhood imagination and dropping them into a gritty city filled with crime, corruption, and a near-noir atmosphere hooked me immediately. It’s an idea that seems unlikely on paper but works impressively well.
What struck me most was how the game treats these characters. They aren't just there for nostalgia or instant recognition, each one gets their own personality, making the universe feel alive. Slowly, you stop seeing them as fairy tale figures and start believing they actually belong in that world.
While the investigation is excellent, it’s the writing that carries everything. The dialogue is memorable, the characters have immense charisma, and the story knows exactly when to surprise you, delivering plot twists that feel completely natural. It’s one of those games where you finish a chapter and immediately want to start the next one.
Now I finally understand why The Wolf Among Us is so well remembered to this day, even after all these years. And if the sequel actually comes out, this time I’m definitely on the hype train too

item.title: Super Mario Odyssey (2017) - ★★★½
item.description:
Not my journey
I don't use this platform to technically review games, there are professionals far more qualified for that. Instead, I use it to document my personal experience with each game within the context of my own life. Writing about how a game made me feel helps me better understand not only the kind of gamer I am, but also who I am as a person.
Replaying Super Mario Odyssey made me realize something interesting: once nostalgia is set aside, the game's greatest strength isn't what resonates with me the most. Its defining characteristic is the constant reinvention of its gameplay. Every new challenge introduces a different mechanic, usually creative and brilliantly executed, that serves a specific purpose before often disappearing for the rest of the game.
I completely understand why Odyssey is so beloved. Its creativity seems limitless, its technical polish is remarkable, the controls are flawless, and its level design is consistently inventive. Still, I realized that my personal taste leans in a different direction.
I tend to prefer games that build themselves around a smaller set of mechanics and spend the entire journey exploring and expanding them. I enjoy the feeling of mastering a system, finishing a game as a better player than when I started. For me, the most rewarding sense of progression isn't just seeing my character grow, it's feeling my own skills evolve alongside them.
The Power Moons do a great job of extending the game's challenges and creating a meaningful post-game. However, their sheer quantity, combined with the relatively small impact they have on progression, made collecting them feel less rewarding over time. When rewards become too frequent, they inevitably lose some of their significance.
In the end, Super Mario Odyssey is still an incredibly fun, creative, and masterfully crafted game. I deeply admire what it sets out to achieve and fully understand why it has become one of the defining platformers of its generation. But for my personal taste, its design philosophy doesn't resonate as much as games that focus on a smaller number of mechanics, developing them with depth and consistency throughout the entire experience. It was a wonderful game to spend time with, but not a journey I believe will stay with me for years to come.

item.title: Hades (2020) - ★★★★
item.description:
When a game wins you over slowly
I first played Hades about two years ago on the Switch. I really liked it, but I didn't quite fall in love with it. With the release of Hades II, I decided to give the original another chance, this time on the PS5, and I ended up enjoying it a lot more. I think this is one of those cases where trophies actually make the game better. Since it's a roguelike, going for the Platinum naturally guides you through the game's optional challenges, giving you a constant reason to keep playing.
I've always had a bit of a hard time getting into roguelikes. In general, they hook me at the beginning and through the middle, but after enough hours, the repetition starts to wear on me. Unless the game keeps rewarding you with meaningful progression, both mechanically and narratively. Those are exactly Hades' greatest strengths.
The gameplay is incredibly engaging, and even after you've "finished" the story by reaching the ending several times, you can still create your own challenges by activating the Pact of Punishment, which lets you add modifiers that make different aspects of the game more difficult.
The story also constantly makes you want to learn more. While I was playing, I found myself watching videos from historians to better understand the characters from Greek mythology and compare their original stories with the game's interpretation. On top of that, the art direction is absolutely gorgeous, from the character designs to the environments.
Hades has definitely climbed much higher on my list of favorite indie games. Now it's time to take a little break after so many hours of playing and finally move on to Hades II.

item.title: Kentucky Route Zero: TV Edition (2020) - ★★★½
item.description:
Like a strange dream
I’m not entirely sure why, but I’ve always had a strong desire to play Kentucky Route Zero. Maybe it’s the intriguing name, the beautiful visuals, or even the cover image of the dog wearing a straw hat. And now that I’ve finally played it… I feel like I still need some time to understand how much of this game will actually stay with me. Right away, what stands out the most are its low-poly graphics and its expressionist art direction, rendered in a minimalist yet vibrant way. Every frame is genuinely striking, something that could easily belong in a contemporary art museum.
It quickly becomes clear that this isn’t a traditional game, not even within the narrative genre. Its inventive mechanics always exist in service of the story, a story that uses magical realism to explore themes like oppression, loneliness, debt, alcoholism, and a new beginnings. These are heav, melancholic themes, and you really need to be in the right mood to follow the journey of Conway, an aging truck driver, and his dog as they search for the mysterious Dogwood Drive to complete his final delivery.
This is one of those games you need to digest, savor, and even research to better understand its story and meanings. Like any work of art, each person will take away something different from it. Nothing is very clear and that’s intentional. It feels like a strange dream you wake up from, trying to piece together what it all meant. There’s also a layer of real world knowledge that enriches the experience. While playing, I found myself researching Kentucky to better grasp the game’s context. For example, the Mammoth Caves, the largest cave system in the world, play an important role in the narrative. Another example is the presence of horses: the region is famous for horse racing, and the game takes this symbol of health and wealth and subverts it into something tied to the destructive impact of capitalism. These small details helped me better understand the narrative, learning the “rules” of that world in order to recognize what’s being subverted. Without that, much of it can feel like just a sequence of surreal images.
On the other hand, not knowing about this need for prior context, combined with the slow pacing of the story (which I understand serves a narrative purpose), made the game feel overly tiring at times. In many moments, I simply didn’t understand what I was looking at, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but it did go a bit too far for me. Maybe I also just wasn’t in the right moment of my life to play it. There were times when I found myself pushing through the story just to finish it, feeling like it dragged. But at the same time, the game stayed on my mind even when I wasn’t playing. I felt frustrated that I wasn’t fully grasping its message and I believe that’s intentional. It wants to create that discomfort. In fact, I think that very ambiguity is what makes it so hard to give it a score… it’s definitely not a game for everyone.

item.title: Souldiers (2022) - ★★½
item.description:
Not every Soulslike hits the mark
I really like souls games, so I went into this one with high expectations ,especially because of the name, hoping for a 2D pixelart soulslike.
And in a way, it is. But in my opinion, in the wrong way. The game leans too heavily on high difficulty, to the point where it feels stiff and restrictive. It lacks truly satisfying moments of exploration and that sense of discovery.
In FromSoftware games, there’s a very well balanced line between difficulty and fairness. You feel like you died because you weren’t good enough yet, which pushes you to learn the mechanics, understand boss patterns, or even take a step back to explore and grow stronger. Here, everything just feels “difficult” in a frustrating way.
The puzzles often don’t make much sense, and the game demands a level of precision that its own mechanics don’t seem to support. I’m not sure if playing on the Switch made things worse, I felt like the controls weren’t as precise as on PS5, but I can only speak from my experience.
Visually, the pixel art is very beautiful, but the world itself feels a bit generic, like a mix of fantasy clichés.
It’s a shame, because the game had everything it needed to be a 4 star RPG, but it gets lost in excess, in this obsession with being difficult. I played for around 70 hours, which is no small amount of time, and for a good portion of it I was already wishing the game would end. I’m not someone who usually drops games, and I pushed through as much as I could, but I couldn’t keep going. At some point, I just wanted to move on to something else.

item.title: Marvel's Spider-Man 2 (2023) - ★★★½
item.description:
Finding joy in a game afraid of boredom
I’ve always felt that Spider-Man games are a bit overrated. They are extremely polished in their mechanics and gameplay, that’s undeniable, but this excessive lack of friction means there’s no frustration, and, on the flip side, not much satisfaction either.
Even when the game introduces a different kind of challenge, it tends to guide you toward the solutions: which buttons to press, where to look, what to do. It’s clearly a series that’s afraid of any kind of boredom, constantly throwing things at you, icons, endless quests…
Structurally, these AAA games are very similar: Spider-Man, Horizon, Ghost of Tsushima, Days Gone… That’s what made me step away from this kind of experience for a while.
That said, every now and then I do feel like playing something like this. As I mentioned, they’re very well-made games mechanically, with good stories, highly cinematic, like big movie blockbusters.
So I went into Spider-Man 2 with that mindset, knowing what to expect and keeping an open mind and I liked it. I know fans tend to prefer the first one, especially because of the story, and although I can see some narrative flaws in this one, as a video game I enjoyed it more.
Even with the usual structure of lots of side quests just to fill your time, I felt that less here. The gameplay and combat felt more dynamic, with more possibilities, and the overall experience was smoother.
It was worth it, it even made me go back and replay the first game to finish the DLCs I hadn’t played yet. And playing the first one more focused on the story, ignoring most of those flashing icons on the map, made it a much better experience too.
This new experience with the Spider-Man games definitely made them go up a bit in my overall perception. The sequence of bosses in the final third, Mr. Negative, Kraven, the symbiote, Scream, and the final boss is very satisfying.

item.title: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild (2017) - ★★★★★
item.description:
A world you live in, not a game you finish
What can be said about a game that’s already so revered? It deserves all the recognition it gets. I can speak from my own experience and the very different feelings I had across the two times I played it. The first was about seven years ago, when I bought the Switch. I had been without a Nintendo console for years and carried a strong sense of nostalgia for the company. I grew up playing the NES, Super Nintendo, and the original Game Boy. So I was eager to see how their experience had evolved over time.
As soon as I got the console, I went straight to the classics: Mario (I’m actually replaying Odyssey right now) and Zelda. I had already heard how incredible and revolutionary the game was, and as I played, I understood why it received so much praise. I understood it on a rational level, but emotionally, my experience felt a bit lukewarm.
It didn’t have that strong sense of progression I was used to, nor those big, defining challenges. The mechanics were technically impressive, and the world was genuinely a joy to explore, but emotionally it felt like a great plateau, not bad, but not great either. I played for over 100 hours and, one day, just stopped. I didn’t even try to defeat Ganon. I had played it, understood why it was special, tried to connect with it… and gave up.
It was like that band you can recognize as talented, but it just doesn’t click with you. You respect it, but you don’t put it on.
And that’s how it stayed for years. I always enjoyed hearing about the game, the things the community discovered, the documentaries about its development but I never felt like going back to it. Until this year, when I decided to give it another shot.
This time, my expectations were better aligned, and I had something I didn’t before: the DLCs. The simple addition of the “Hero’s Path” completely changed the experience. The near absence of map markers is brilliant, but before, I spent a lot of time feeling lost, unsure of where I had already been. That feeling was interesting at first, but eventually became frustrating.
With “Hero’s Path,” I was able to plan better, create my own goals, and explore the map in a more structured way. On top of that, the challenge modes brought the level of difficulty I felt was missing in my first playthrough, which ended up highlighting all the qualities the game is known for.
It was a completely different experience. Even after almost 10 years, the game feels even more impressive. Being more aware of my actions helped me get lost less unintentionally and allowed me to connect more with the stories, the side quests, and the NPCs.
It’s a phenomenal game, one you could live in forever. It’s not a game you “finish”; it’s a game you eventually choose to stop playing because you have to move on to other things.

item.title: Octopath Traveler II (2023) - ★★★★
item.description:
A journey of many emotions
It’s hard to evaluate this game because I feel like I experienced many different emotions throughout my journey.
At first, it brought back that feeling of playing with toys as a kid, when you’d mix different worlds and characters with no rules, like LEGO, Playmobil, He-Man, Rambo… everything together. In Octopath Traveler II, that comes through in the variety of classes, Warrior, Dancer, Merchant, Scholar, Cleric, Thief, Hunter, Apothecary and also in the game’s tone, which is quite naive and simple in its premise, where the power of friendship and even a good conversation can solve complex problems. I really loved that. Combined with the very traditional turn-based combat system, it felt like pure nostalgia. Up to this point, it’s a solid 5/5.
The combat may seem simple at first, but as the game progresses, there are significant difficulty spikes that force you to improve constantly. Not just mastering the battle mechanics, but also carefully thinking about your party composition, skill combinations, and the jobs you choose for each situation. I felt a big jump in difficulty midway through the game, in the final boss, and especially in the hardest optional boss, Galdera (I had to use a guide to beat it).
The main downside for me is the excessive number of random encounters. They happen within seconds while you’re exploring the map. A lot of the time, I didn’t mind, after all, combat is the core of the game, but when I wanted to explore an area, reach hidden chests, or simply navigate more complex maps, it became frustrating. Often, you’re already overleveled for a region, so the battles aren’t even challenging or interesting anymore, and this happens quite frequently.
On top of that, as is common in this type of game, even with so many random encounters, you still need to grind at certain points. In a 140-hour game, that can start to feel tiring.
On the other hand, the tougher battles are extremely challenging and very rewarding when you finally overcome them. Many require such specific strategies and combinations that, in some cases, I could only figure them out by looking things up online. It almost feels like the developers designed it that way, because even if you explore thoroughly and complete side quests, it’s still easy to miss important elements.
In the end, I’d say the overall experience is positive. I’ll definitely miss these characters and the journey they gave me.

item.title: Mega Man 11 (2018) - ★★★★
item.description:
For me, Mega Man is synonymous with video games. It brings back memories from the very beginning of my gaming life, all the way back in the ’80s.
I played a lot of Mega Man 1, 2, and X back then, but I didn’t really follow the series as it evolved over the years. Some time ago, I decided to try Mega Man 11, curious to see how it had changed after all this time. To my surprise, it was… hard. Really hard. Maybe I just wasn’t in the right mindset at the time, but I ended up putting it aside and waiting for the right moment.
And when that moment came, I picked it up again,this time with adjusted expectations, and I completely fell into it. That classic Mega Man experience is still there: memorable bosses, the “puzzle” of figuring out which weapon works best against each one, the character design, and of course, the difficulty—especially at the beginning, when you don’t have any extra weapons or abilities.
It was a joy to play, both fun and nostalgic. Going after the platinum challenges (I’m still missing two trophies) makes everything even more engaging and rewarding.
Long live Mega Man.

item.title: Bloodborne (2015) - ★★★★★
item.description:
Remains an unmatched masterpiece
Even though I played it late, in the 2000s, Bloodborne is one of the games of my life. It was the game that introduced me to FromSoftware’s souls‑likes, which became my favorite subgenre. After it came Demon’s Souls, Dark Souls 1, 2 and 3, and Elden Ring. I loved those games so much I ended up platinum‑trophying them, and a nagging thought settled in my gamer brain: “you still haven’t platinumed Bloodborne.” Years went by until I decided to put that to rest. I did two more runs to platinum it: I needed two different endings and to kill Yharnam, Pthumerian Queen in the Chalice Dungeons.
Here I want to focus more on this second experience after so many years and after playing a lot more souls games. Everyone already knows the game’s importance: its unique atmosphere and the long wait from fans for a possible sequel that may never come.
One thing that surprised me on the second playthrough was how much easier the game felt than I remembered from my first time, years of training and experience with other games really make a difference. On the third run, when I just wanted the last ending and went straight through the main story without doing side content and knowing exactly where to go, I realized how short the game can be, really short. I think it didn’t even take 10 hours, which blew my mind since my first time must have been over 50 hours.
Anyway, I still think Bloodborne is everything people say it is and it remains at the top of my favorite games list, an incredible game. My next challenge now is to platinum the only one left: Sekiro, which I plan to play later this year.

item.title: Hot Wheels Unleashed 2: Turbocharged (2023) - ★★★
item.description:
I haven’t played a racing game in quite a while, but I suddenly felt like trying something fast, dynamic, and unpretentious. I gave Hot Wheels Unleashed 2: Turbocharged a shot on PSN and didn’t regret it at all, it was exactly what I was looking for, and I even found it more challenging than I expected.
In the end, it was a light and enjoyable experience, but I can’t help seeing some wasted potential. Given the theme, the racing focus, and the strength of the Hot Wheels brand, it could have been a much more special game. Still, not every game needs to be special, some are just there to satisfy a craving for something different. It definitely left me feeling motivated to dive back into more racing games again. 🏎️

item.title: Silent Hill 2 (2024) - ★★★★
item.description:
After finishing Alan Wake 2, I decided to continue the horror streak with Silent Hill 2. I never played the original back in the day, but it’s one of those games everyone says you have to experience at least once in your life.
Over the years, I built an image of what Silent Hill 2 was supposed to be, a profound story with a heavy atmosphere that makes you feel and reflect on what it means to be human. And while that idea wasn’t wrong, actually playing it is a completely different experience. It’s much harder to absorb than I expected.
I couldn’t play for long sessions. Everything felt so brutal emotionally and visually. Even the minimalist gameplay serves the story perfectly: nothing is missing, nothing is excessive. The constant darkness pulls you in, forcing you to pay full attention if you want to move forward in the narrative.
Silent Hill 2 is the kind of game that keeps you wanting to dig deeper. What really happened with James and Mary? Who exactly is Maria? What’s the backstory behind Laura and Eddie? And what’s going on with the town of Silent Hill itself was any of it real, or just James’s guilt manifesting around him?
In the end, I don’t think having the “right” answer matters. What stays with you is the journey and the reflections it leaves behind. It’s a game that lingers with you long after the credits roll.

item.title: Thank Goodness You're Here! (2024) - ★★★½
item.description:
A great palate-cleaner of a game, perfect to play between bigger, more demanding titles. Funny, charming, and very short (around 4 hours long), it delivers a narrative experience packed with sharp, sarcastic British humor as it portrays the daily life of a fictional English small town.
The gameplay is simple: basically jump and slap. With just these actions, you explore a world full of eccentric characters, bizarre situations, and wonderfully absurd, surreal moments. All of this comes wrapped in a gorgeous, stylized art direction that resembles a mix of Cartoon Network, The Simpsons, Family Guy, and a dash of Monty Python.
It’s absolutely worth experiencing: short, different, and memorable.
